Article Title: Steve Jobs’ son watched his father battle cancer as a child; decades later, Reed Jobs is using a $1 billion fund to fight the disease
Article Text:
Reed Jobs’ childhood changed after Steve Jobs’ diagnosis

Yosemite now manages more than $1 billion

Reed Jobs wants cancer to become manageable

The Yosemite name has a personal connection

Reed Jobs was 12 when his father, Apple co-founder Steve Jobs, was diagnosed with a rare form of pancreatic cancer. Eight years later, Steve died at 56, while Reed was an undergraduate at Stanford. The experience shaped Reed’s interest in cancer research, leading him to spend summers working in oncology laboratories as a teenager before eventually moving into healthcare investing. In 2023, he launched Yosemite, an oncology-focused investment firm that combines venture capital with philanthropic funding. Yosemite initially launched with more than $200 million. By early 2026, the firm had raised another $200 million-plus for its second fund and said it was managing more than $1 billion in assets.Reed became interested in cancer after seeing his father diagnosed when he was 12. Steve Jobs had been diagnosed with a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour, a rare form of pancreatic cancer. Reed later spent time working in oncology laboratories at Stanford as a teenager and initially entered Stanford as a pre-med student.Steve Jobs died on October 5, 2011, at the age of 56. Reed was 20 at the time and was studying at Stanford.After his father's death, Reed changed his major from pre-med to history. He eventually returned to healthcare through his work at Emerson Collective, the impact-investing and philanthropic organisation founded by his mother, Laurene Powell Jobs.Before creating Yosemite, Reed spent years working at Emerson Collective, where he focused on health and cancer-related initiatives. Yosemite emerged from that work and became an independent organisation in 2023.The firm announced its first close of more than $200 million in August 2023. Its model combines traditional venture investment with philanthropic grants for academic researchers. The aim is to support scientific work at an early stage and help promising discoveries develop into treatments and companies.Yosemite focuses exclusively on oncology and has invested in areas including gene therapy, immunotherapy, cancer vaccines, radiopharmaceuticals, artificial intelligence-powered drug discovery and earlier cancer detection.Yosemite's financial scale has grown substantially since its launch. In January 2026, the San Francisco Chronicle reported that the firm had raised more than $200 million for its second fund and was seeking an additional $150 million. The new fund was backed by institutions and investors including Amgen, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, MIT and John Doerr.Forbes reported that Yosemite's second fund was targeting $350 million. Following its latest funding round, the firm said it managed more than $1 billion in assets, including money overseen for hospitals, endowments and foundations.The firm's own announcement said its second fund had initially closed at more than $200 million and that Yosemite now managed more than $1 billion in assets.Reed has described a long-term goal of changing how cancer is treated. In an interview reported by the San Francisco Chronicle, he said he believes many cancers could eventually move from being fatal diagnoses to manageable, chronic diseases within his lifetime. Yosemite's current investments reflect that strategy. The firm has backed companies working on technologies ranging from gene therapies and cancer vaccines to AI-assisted drug discovery. According to the San Francisco Chronicle, Yosemite was invested in about 20 companies and expected its new fund to support around 25 companies.The name of Reed's firm also comes from an important chapter in his family's history. Steve Jobs and Laurene Powell Jobs married on March 18, 1991, at the Ahwahnee Hotel in Yosemite National Park. The ceremony was attended by about 50 people, and the wedding included a vegan cake shaped like Half Dome. The couple also went hiking after the ceremony. Reed was born in September 1991, months after his parents' wedding. He was their first child, followed by daughters Erin and Eve.Reed's career has therefore come full circle. His interest in oncology began during his father's illness, continued through his teenage work in cancer laboratories and later became part of his professional work at Emerson Collective.
Article Summary: Reed Jobs was 12 when his father, Apple co-founder Steve Jobs, was diagnosed with a rare form of pancreatic cancer. The experience shaped Reed’s interest in cancer research, leading him to spend summers working in oncology laboratories as a teenager. In 2023, he launched Yosemite, an oncologist-focused investment firm that combines venture capital with philanthropic funding. By early 2026, the firm had raised another $200 million-plus for its second fund and said it was managing more than $1 billion in assets.

Article Title: JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon once again 'warns' Europe 'you may be losing', offers 'big, beautiful solution'
Article Text:
Jamie Dimon calls for deeper economic integration

What Europe needs to fix, according to Jamie Dimon

Vision for a stronger Western alliance

Not the first time JPMorgan CEO delivered this message

Jamie Dimon, the CEO of America’s largest bank JPMorgan Chase has renewed his warning that Europe risks falling behind economically, while proposing what he called a ‘big beautiful’ free-trade agreement with the United States as part of a broader effort to strengthen the Western alliance. In an opinion piece published in The Wall Street Journal, Dimon argued that Washington should offer Europe a sweeping economic partnership if the continent implements meaningful economic and military reforms designed to boost growth, competitiveness and security. “I believe the U.S. should offer Europe a major inducement: If it executes meaningful economic and military reforms... the US will negotiate one big, beautiful economic and free-trade agreement with Europe,” Dimon wrote.According to Dimon, such an agreement would go beyond Europe and could eventually be extended to friendly democracies including Canada, Mexico, Japan, South Korea, Australia and the Philippines.He described deeper economic integration among democratic allies as a potential “game changer” that would allow them to set global trade rules, strengthen economic resilience and present a united front against geopolitical pressures.Dimon's proposal contrasts with the more protectionist approach adopted by the administration of Donald Trump, whose tariff policies have strained relations with several trading partners, including the European Union and Canada.Dimon's op-ed didn't just float a vague aspiration — it named specific reforms he believes are prerequisites. He called on the European Union to finally complete its long-delayed Capital Markets Union and Banking Union to boost competitiveness, to follow through on the recommendations laid out in the Draghi report, and to secure genuine independence in defense, manufacturing, and energy.He argued that a Europe capable of mobilizing capital, scaling innovative companies, consolidating defense production, and reducing strategic dependencies would emerge as a stronger security partner, a more resilient economic partner, and a more credible counterweight to China's growing economic influence.Beyond Europe, Dimon argued that the United States must also take steps to preserve its position as the world's leading economic and military power. He called for renewed focus on strengthening the American economy, expanding opportunity and reinforcing democratic alliances.According to Dimon, a combination of US leadership and successful European reforms could create a stronger Western bloc capable of driving economic growth and addressing long-term geopolitical challenges.“A renewed commitment to American values and alliances coupled with bold reforms by Europe would be a geopolitical and economic home run, guaranteeing the Western world's strength for the next 250 years,” he wrote.This isn't the first time Dimon has bluntly criticized Europe's economic standing. Last year, speaking to European business and political leaders at an event in Ireland, he delivered an even more direct version of the same warning, telling the room flatly that, compared with the US and Asia, Europe is losing.
Article Summary: JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon has called for a 'big beautiful' free-trade agreement with the United States. Dimon argued that Washington should offer Europe a sweeping economic partnership if the continent implements meaningful economic and military reforms. According to Dimon, such an agreement would go beyond Europe and could eventually be extended to friendly democracies including Canada, Mexico and Japan.

Article Title: In 2010, Elon Musk funded a 25-kilowatt solar system for an Alabama disaster centre; 108 panels and battery backup were designed to keep it powered when the surrounding grid went down
Article Text:
“This seemed like a good thing to do to help people out, while simultaneously creating awareness that there was a better way to keep things going than just ‘drill, baby, drill,”

A solar system for a community recovering from disasters

“Electricity bills are a big deal for a community center like ours when you have to pay for it out-of-pocket,”

“But all of a sudden now we have solar power! For a little area that no one has ever heard about, that’s amazing.”

The project led to wider solar efforts

Elon Musk funded a solar project in Alabama in 2010. The 25-kilowatt system, installed at the South Bay Communities Alliance (SBCA) Hurricane Response Center in Coden, Alabama, was designed to help the facility keep operating if a disaster knocked out the surrounding electricity grid. The installation included 108 photovoltaic panels and battery backup and was expected to provide about 90% to 100% of the centre’s electricity needs. Musk’s foundation provided the funding, while solar company SolarCity donated and installed the system. The project came as Coden was still dealing with the effects of Hurricane Katrina and the Deepwater Horizon oil spill, which had affected the coastal community’s commercial fishing industry.Musk said the project was intended to help residents while demonstrating an alternative to dependence on oil.said Musk, who also runs the electric car company Tesla Motors.Coden was a coastal community where commercial fishing had been an important source of employment.The Deepwater Horizon disaster added another setback to an area that was already recovering from Hurricane Katrina. More than 100 families in the community were still waiting to rebuild their homes after the hurricane.The SBCA Hurricane Response Center served as a gathering and response point for the local community. The solar installation was intended to keep the centre powered during emergencies, when a damaged grid could leave residents without electricity.The system was also expected to reduce the centre’s regular electricity costs.says Zack Carter, an organiser for SBCA.The battery backup was important because this project was more than just producing power in the normal way. It was supposed to provide energy security if a hurricane or other disaster knocked out the local power grid.The Coden installation became an early disaster-relief project involving SolarCity and the Musk Foundation. The organisations later worked on a similar solar project in Japan following the 2011 Fukushima nuclear disaster. In 2012, SolarCity also worked with partners to provide portable solar power stations for communities affected by Hurricane Sandy.By then, SolarCity’s philanthropy had expanded well beyond disaster relief. In 2013, the company launched the GivePower Foundation to provide electricity to schools in developing countries without reliable power.By 2014, GivePower said it had helped 511 schools in Africa and Central America, exceeding its original target of 400 schools. Its projects used solar panels, batteries and lights, while teams also trained local residents to troubleshoot the equipment and maintain the systems.The organisation's projects included schools in Mali, Nicaragua and Kenya. In Kenya, a school in the village of Kirindon could use laptops donated by Intel after receiving a solar installation.For Coden, however, the original project had a more immediate purpose. The combination of 108 solar panels and battery storage was intended to give a disaster response centre a source of electricity that could continue working even when the surrounding grid could not.
Article Summary: Elon Musk funded a solar project in Alabama in 2010. The 25-kilowatt system was designed to help the facility keep operating if a disaster knocked out the surrounding electricity grid. The installation included 108 photovoltaic panels and battery backup and was expected to provide about 90% to 100% of the centre's electricity needs.

Article Title: Zoho launches Arattai-for-Business app; offers free messaging for healthcare, education
Article Text:
Zoho launches Arattai-for-Business app; offers free messaging for healthcare, education

Arattai Business Platform launched

Free messages for healthcare and education

Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu has announced the launch of Arattai-for-Business, a new app that allows businesses to communicate with their customers through Arattai. The company is also launching the Arattai Business Platform, which will allow businesses to connect their existing software and automation systems with the messaging platform. Sridhar Vembu shared the announcement in a post, saying, “The Arattai-for-Business app is live. This app allows businesses to communicate with customers.”Along with the business app, Zoho is introducing the Arattai Business Platform to help organisations connect their business software and automation systems with Arattai.The platform is also being offered free to government and public services. Vembu specifically mentioned services such as the Railways.“The Arattai Business Platform is free for government and public services like Railways. We are working on those integrations right now,” Sridhar Vembu wrote in the post.The company is currently working on integrations that could allow government and public service organisations to use Arattai for communication with users.Zoho is also offering a free messaging allowance to healthcare and educational institutions.Sridhar Vembu said, “In addition, for healthcare and educational institutions, we give a free allowance of 1 milllion messages per month.”The announcement expands Arattai beyond its consumer messaging use and adds features aimed at organisations that need to communicate with large numbers of customers or users.Arattai is Zoho's messaging platform and competes in a market dominated by established messaging services. The latest business-focused launch gives companies and institutions a way to connect customer communication with their existing software and automation systems.The announcement did not provide details about pricing for businesses beyond the free provisions mentioned for government services, healthcare and educational institutions. It also did not specify when the planned Railway and other public-service integrations will be completed.The Arattai-for-Business app is live. This app allows businesses to communicate with customers.Along with it, we are also launching the Arattai Business Platform to integrate your business software and automation systems with Arattai. The Arattai Business Platform is free for government and public services like Railways. We are working on those integrations right now.In addition, for healthcare and educational institutions, we give a free allowance of 1 milllion messages per month.
Article Summary: Zoho launches Arattai-for-Business app; offers free messaging for healthcare, education. The company is also launching theArattai Business Platform, which will allow businesses to connect their existing software and automation systems with the messaging platform. Zoho is also offering a free messaging allowance to healthcare and educational institutions.

Article Title: BMW wants AI to do its managers' jobs, plans 20% layoffs across divisions and leadership roles; CEO says: We're improving our...
Article Text:
BMW bets on AI to replace managers, up to 8,000 jobs hit in Germany

BMW wants agentic AI running everything from car development to aftersales

Falling margins and a China slump are forcing BMW to rethink its strategy

BMW is putting artificial intelligence at the centre of its turnaround plan, and the first thing it will reshape is its own management. The German luxury carmaker said it will cut its divisions and the management roles tied to them by 20% by mid-2027. A comparable reduction will follow at the organisational levels below. The logic, as BMW explained it to investors, is that AI will make the company more agile, so it will need fewer layers of managers.The plan was unveiled at BMW's capital markets day on Wednesday (September 30), held across its Gut Schwaerzenbach retreat in Bavaria and its Munich headquarters. It was the first big investor test for CEO Milan Nedeljkovic, a former BMW trainee and production head who took charge in May. "We are improving our structures and cost base so we can meet the increasingly fierce competition that will define this industry in the coming years," Nedeljkovic said, adding that the workforce restructuring programme is "an important lever for this. "The cuts build on a deal BMW reached with labour representatives in July. That plan, based on voluntary departures, could affect up to 8,000 white-collar employees in Germany.That is about 5% of a global workforce that stood at just under 155,000 at the end of 2025. BMW's presentation also confirmed a 20% reduction in senior vice presidents.BMW plans to push AI deeper into vehicle development, material purchasing, sales and marketing, and aftersales. CFO Walter Mertl called consistent use of agentic AI across the company "a game-changer" for faster development, leaner structures and quicker decisions.The groundwork is already in place. BMW runs more than 600 AI use cases across its business. Engineers use AI to run crash simulations without building physical prototypes, while procurement teams use it to analyse supplier contracts and draft tender documents.Few large companies name AI as plainly when announcing job cuts. BMW now joins UPS, which cut 12,000 managers, and Lufthansa, which plans to shed 4,000 administrative jobs by the end of the decade. Nedeljkovic, however, maintains that "it's not a cost-savings programme."The numbers explain the urgency. BMW's automotive margin slipped to 2.3% in its latest results, down from 5.3% in 2025. In June, the company issued its third China-linked profit warning in just over three years, saying margins could fall to as low as 1% this year. Its shares have lost more than a third of their value over the past year.BMW now targets a 3% to 5% margin in 2028, with a return to its 8% to 10% range by the early 2030s. Chinese buyers shifting to local brands like BYD, US tariffs and high energy costs have hit German carmakers hard, and Volkswagen and Mercedes-Benz are cutting costs too.The lineup is changing by region as well. Europe gets an entry-level electric car on the Neue Klasse platform from 2028, while the US gets a new high-end SUV. In China, BMW will localise more production, lean on local partners for autonomous driving and software, and weigh exports of China-built cars to Southeast Asia. It has also skipped this month's Paris motor show.BMW says more measures are under evaluation, with decisions due by spring 2027. The 20% management cut, in other words, may only be the first round.
Article Summary: BMW will cut its divisions and management roles tied to them by 20% by mid-2027. The logic is that AI will make the company more agile, so it will need fewer layers of managers. BMW joins UPS, which cut 12,000 managers, and Lufthansa, which plans to shed 4,000 administrative jobs.

Article Title: When Steve Jobs 'hid' his Porsche as he didn't want to make NeXT, the company Apple bought years later, look like ...
Article Text:
The day Steve Jobs ‘hid’ his Porsche

John Ternus and his the 700-horsepower Porsche 935

Engineering Roots and High-Performance DNA

While they are all on the same page when it comes to the company’s products, two of Apple’s CEOs across the decades have opposite approaches to the same German sports car maker. Back in 1987, Steve Jobs rushed to hide his Porsche ahead of an investor pitch because he didn't want his struggling startup, NeXT, to look flush with cash. Nearly forty years later, Apple’s newly appointed chief executive, John Ternus, owns one of the rarest track-only Porsches ever built, and regularly pushes it to its limits on California racetracks.The story of Jobs’ car cover-up dates to his post-Apple venture, NeXT, which Apple eventually acquired years later to form the software base of OS X. According to former NeXT engineer Randy Adams, Jobs came running into the workspace right before billionaire businessman Ross Perot arrived for an investment meeting:“Randy, we have to hide the Porsches,” Jobs said.Up until that morning, Jobs and Adams had been parking their personal vehicles diagonally across three parking stalls to safeguard the paint from door dings. Concerned that pulling up to an office flanked by luxury sports cars would give Perot the impression that the young enterprise did not need cash, Jobs had the vehicles moved out of sight behind NeXT's Palo Alto building.The low-profile appearance did the trick: Perot went on to inject $20 million into the company.While Jobs viewed his car as a financial signal that needed to disappear during negotiations, Ternus engages with the brand in an entirely different setting: amateur motorsport. According to Motor1, Ternus owns one of only 77 units of the track-exclusive Porsche 935. Based on the 991-generation 911 GT2 RS, the vehicle carries an original base price topping $800,000 (€701,948 before taxes) and packs serious mechanical muscle.Its engine output is 700 horsepower via a 3.8-liter twin-turbocharged flat-six and it has a lightweight frame of 3,042 pounds (around 1380 kg). It is not street-legal and lacks conventional race championship homologation, making it strictly an instrument for private track events, Clubsport sessions and driver clinics.Rather than locking the vehicle away in a showroom as a static financial asset, Ternus runs the car at WeatherTech Raceway Laguna Seca. As reported by The Wall Street Journal, he has clocked lap times under 1 minute and 40 seconds – a quick pace for a non-professional driver.Ternus’s passion for circuit racing mirrors his technical background. Before stepping into the CEO role on September 1, 2026, he built his career through mechanical engineering. He graduated with a mechanical engineering degree from the University of Pennsylvania, worked as a mechanical engineer prior to joining Apple in 2001; Promoted to vice president of hardware engineering in 2013 and joined Apple’s executive leadership team in 2021.An active follower of Formula 1 and competitive motorsport, with Apple services head Eddy Cue previously highlighting Ternus’s participation in amateur track driving.While Jobs saw the sports car as an image liability to conceal behind an office wall, Ternus treats the ultra-rare machine as an engineering outlet.
Article Summary: Steve Jobs hid his Porsche ahead of an investor pitch because he didn't want his startup, NeXT, to look flush with cash. Nearly forty years later, Apple’s newly appointed chief executive, John Ternus, owns one of the rarest track-only Porsches ever built.

Article Title: Elon Musk's 'tip' to tech CEOs: Best way to test 'safety' of your AI models is to put them on a Delta flight, as ...
Article Text:
Earlier this week, Elon Musk warned that Delta will ‘lose a lot of customers’

Elon Musk warns Delta will ‘lose a lot of customers’

Delta Airlines on why it rejected Elon Musk’s Starlink

Elon Musk has humorously suggested that the best way to test the safety of AI models is by placing them on a Delta flight, implying that the airline's in-flight WiFi is so unreliable it effectively cuts off internet access. Sharing a post on X (formerly Twitter), Musk wrote:“Best way to sandbox an AI is to put it on a Delta flight – it will have no chance of accessing the Internet!”. The comments come as Delta Airlines opted against Starlink in favour of Amazon Leo for in-flight internet service. According to latest reports, Delta CEO Ed Bastian cited Elon Musk as the reason to skip Starlink. An X user JonNYC allegedly cited the Delta CEO saying “We do not want to be with Elon Musk”.In a post on September 28, X user John LeFevre said that Delta's rival United Airlines Holdings Inc. had 600+ aircraft with Starlink. The figure represented approximately 36% of the airline's entire fleet. "Delta has zero, and no plans for it. People will book accordingly. RIP Delta," he wrote in the post. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk responded to the post writing: “Delta will lose a lot of customers”.Delta Airlines is reportedly targeting 2028 to start offering Leo in-flight Wi-Fi on about half of its fleet. As quoted in a post by X user Sawyer Meritt earlier this year, Delta Airlines explained why it chose Amazon’s Leo saying:“This agreement gives us the fastest and most cost-effective technology available to better connect the world today, and it deepens our work with a global leader that shares our ambition to build what’s next.”In a statement to PC Mag then, the airline said “The assertion in question is not accurate”, claiming that incorporating Delta Sync with Starlink would have been permitted under SpaceX's in-flight Wi-Fi agreement. It further stated that it want to deepen work with “a global leader that shares our ambition to build what’s next.”
Article Summary: Elon Musk suggests best way to test the safety of AI models is by placing them on a Delta flight. Comments come as Delta Airlines opted against Starlink in favour of Amazon Leo for in-flight internet service. According to latest reports, Delta CEO Ed Bastian cited Elon Musk as the reason to skip Starlink.

Article Title: The next thing Adidas wants to make bespoke is the foam itself
Article Text:
An early prototype of Adidas's printed foam at the APEX Lab in Herzogenaurach

A foot model recreated from APEX scan data, used to build Project R.A.P. footwear

Running shoes have spent a decade getting faster through chemistry

Adidas's printed foam changes how it compresses through its structure, not a new formula

The Futurecraft 4D midsole, printed by Carbon as a lattice rather than moulded from foam. (Picture: Adidas)

Printed foam gets its behaviour from geometry

One of five printed foam versions Adidas made in three weeks.

The printed foam's underside, with openings that change in size and density from heel to toe.

Without a mould, foam can be remade for every athlete

Adidas's printed foam prototypes, which can be remade for each athlete without a mould.

Running-shoe foam has changed a great deal over the past decade, but it is still made in moulds, and a moulded midsole behaves the same way for every runner who wears that size. Adidas has been 3D-printing midsoles for close to a decade to get around that, though it has printed them from resin rather than foam.At its headquarters in Herzogenaurach, Adidas has now shown foam that comes out of a printer. It was the final stop at the APEX Lab during Home of Innovation, the company's name for a tour through the labs where athletes test products most people won't see for another year or two. Chief Creative Officer Alasdhair Willis calls it "a future continuously being built." APEX, short for Athlete Product Excellence, is the elite-only room where Adidas makes bespoke products for its biggest names.Most of the tables there dealt with how a shoe gets customised to a single athlete. One covered the profile APEX builds before anything is made: 3D body and foot scans, pressure mapping and gait analysis, the process behind boots and shoes made for Lionel Messi, Anthony Edwards, Noah Lyles and Alexander Zverev.Another held Project R.A.P., short for Radical Athlete Perception, Adidas's 3D-printed footwear platform.Its lattice boots are made from an athlete's scan data and worn in MLS matches by Philadelphia Union's Cavan Sullivan, and its basketball shoes by Brooklyn Nets rookie Mikel Brown Jr.The last table came with a warning. Mateo, the designer behind it, said the project was at a very early stage, much further from production than R.A.P., and that the group was the first outside Adidas to see it. What he showed was printed foam, in structures that could be tuned in ways a moulded midsole cannot.Foam sits under almost every athletic shoe, but running is where the race to improve it has been fought most openly. For most of the last decade, progress in running-shoe cushioning has been a materials race. EVA, the light and cheap foam that sat under most shoes for years, gave way to expanded TPU, which Adidas brought to market as Boost in 2013. The next jump came from PEBA-based foams, which are lighter and return more energy, and which now sit under most elite racing shoes.Each step came from a lab working on the formula. A better foam meant a new polymer, a new blend or a new way of expanding it. Engineers could shape a midsole, stack layers or add a carbon plate, but the foam inside a moulded midsole behaves more or less the same throughout. Changing how it compresses has meant changing what it is made of.There is a practical reason for that. Foam midsoles are moulded, and a mould can only produce shapes that can be pulled back out of it. Complex internal structures are off the table, so the chemistry has had to carry most of the load.Adidas has found a way around that limit before. In 2017 it introduced Futurecraft 4D with Carbon, a printed midsole that gets its cushioning from a lattice structure, and 2021's 4DFWD added bowtie-shaped cells coded to compress forward under vertical impact. Those midsoles are printed as an elastomeric lattice, not foam in the EVA or Boost sense, so Adidas has been able to shape cushioning through geometry for some years, though never in foam.Mateo described printed foam as a combination of two things. From additive manufacturing it takes precision, control and customisation. From foam it keeps lightness, energy return and deformation, which he called a fancy word for how squishy it is. Adidas had to develop a new additive method to make it, though Mateo didn't say what the base material is.He was wearing one of the structures, so he walked up and down beside the table to show it working. This design is meant to maximise vertical deformation, meaning how far the foam compresses under load, and it does that by collapsing forward as the runner moves. You could see the cells fold in a set direction rather than squashing evenly, as a moulded slab would.The idea of a midsole that folds forward will be familiar from 4DFWD, which produced that movement with printed resin. The structure Mateo was wearing does it in foam, with the arrangement of its cells deciding how it compresses. He said this design was only one example, and a different structure could be optimised for weight, or built for walking rather than running, from the same material. A basketball shoe has to absorb heavy landings and support sharp cuts, while a walking shoe needs comfort over hours rather than speed over minutes. If the structure decides how the foam behaves, one printed material could in principle be shaped for each of those jobs.Geometry becomes more useful once it can be adjusted for an individual. Mateo said the lab can collect an athlete's pressure data, kinematics and foot scans, and then tune the structures to that athlete. That hasn't been possible with foam before, because a moulded midsole comes out the same for everyone in a size. APEX already profiles athletes across football, basketball, tennis and running, so the data needed to shape foam for one person is being collected well beyond runners.Speed matters as much as precision. Three weeks before the session, Mateo was at the factory where the samples on the table were made, and he produced five versions of the structure, each tuned differently. The process he described was simple: make a pair, test it with the athlete in the lab, adjust it, make another pair, and narrow down to the best shoe for that athlete.Alexander Taylor, Adidas's Senior Vice President of Innovation Design & Concepts, who was leading the group, put that pace in context. With conventional manufacturing, each change means working on moulds, and the structures on Mateo's table could not be moulded in the first place. Mateo has practically been living at the factory for the past three or four months, Taylor said, because the project now moves as quickly as he can test it. The shoes also look different, since the process produces shapes nothing from a mould would.For now, the project is being judged by how the structures behave rather than by numbers. Mateo didn't share energy-return figures to compare against moulded foams, and at this stage there may not be finished ones to share.Printed foam is still a long way behind R.A.P., which already has boots on an MLS pitch. If it follows the same path, its first wearers will be the athletes whose profiles are already on file at APEX, a few steps from the table where it was shown.
Article Summary: Adidas has been 3D-printing midsoles for close to a decade to get around that. It has printed them from resin rather than foam. At its headquarters in Herzogenaurach, Adidas has now shown foam that comes out of a printer.

Article Title: In 2018, Elon Musk donated $480,350 for Flint school water filters; four years later, redesigned systems allowed students to drink from fountains again after years of relying on alternative supplies
Article Text:
In 2018, Elon Musk donated $480,350 for Flint school water filters; four years later, redesigned systems allowed students to drink from fountains again after years of relying on alternative supplies

How the new water filters work

Why did the project take four years

For four years, students at Flint Community Schools relied on bottled and delivered water instead of drinking directly from school fountains. That is now changing after new ultraviolet water filtration systems were installed and tested across the district. The project dates back to 2018, when Elon Musk donated $480,350 to help install water filtration stations following the Flint water crisis. The upgraded systems are designed to remove lead, bacteria and other metals from water before it reaches students. District officials say testing found no detectable lead or harmful bacteria after filtration, allowing the drinking stations to be used again.A total of 130 filtration stations have been installed across Flint's 11 schools and administration building. The systems use three stages of filtration. Water first passes through an activated carbon filter designed to remove lead, copper and other particles. It then goes through an ultrafilter to remove most bacteria. Finally, ultraviolet light is used to kill remaining bacteria and viruses.Testing found lead levels before filtration varied by school. The highest average was 219 parts per billion (ppb) at Accelerated Learning Academy, while one test at Scott Elementary recorded 620 ppb.The US Environmental Protection Agency's recommended action level is 15 ppb.After filtration, tests found no detectable lead or harmful bacteria at the tested sites.The stations were installed during the 2019-20 school year, but researchers found problems with the original filters during testing. The systems produced inconsistent results and were not certified to meet National Sanitation Foundation standards.Researchers later redesigned the systems and began testing new units in 2021.Superintendent Kevelin Jones said students can now drink from the hydration stations, but the district will continue providing bottled water for the rest of the school year as some families may still have concerns.“I am very excited,” Superintendent Kevelin Jones said. “It was about four years ago where we were talking about this, and this was in the early stages. ... To see that it came into fruition and our scholars can now drink water out of those hydration stations is a win for us,” Jones said.The district also plans regular testing and filter replacements to monitor water quality.
Article Summary: In 2018, Elon Musk donated $480,350 for Flint school water filters; four years later, redesigned systems allowed students to drink from fountains again. The upgraded systems are designed to remove lead, bacteria and other metals from water before it reaches students. District officials say testing found no detectable lead or harmful bacteria after filtration, allowing the drinking stations to be used again.

Article Title: Ford CEO Jim Farley makes clear distinction of the jobs that AI cannot replace; says automation cannot be done for ...
Article Text:
AI cannot automate practical judgement, says Ford CEO

Line between engineer and technician is blurring

Already happening inside Ford

Trust remains critical for AI adoption

An old tension in a new form

Poll Vote & Share your view Which of the following job roles do you think will be least affected by AI? Electricians and technicians Finance analysts Call center representatives 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Ford CEO Jim Farley has made a clear distinction between the types of jobs artificial intelligence is likely to replace and the ones that will remain dependent on human expertise, arguing that skilled trades workers will largely be protected from the first wave of AI disruption. According to a report by Fortune, speaking during a backstage media roundtable at Ford Pro Accelerate, Farley emphasised that AI would increasingly function as a ‘companion’ for workers in factories, repair shows and skilled-trades occupations instead of a replacement. “I think most of these jobs will be both using AI and also protected from it,” Farley said. However, he warned that more routine white-collar roles face greater disruption. “If you work in finance doing spreadsheets, or you're in a call centre, or you're an entry-level programmer, those jobs are definitely going to be changed and eliminated with at least this first inning of AI.”Farley argued that AI is likely to struggle to replace workers whose jobs require hands-on problem-solving, physical expertise and real-world judgement. Electricians, technicians, mechanics and factory skilled-trades workers will continue to be needed even as automation becomes more advanced, he said.According to Farley, these roles will increasingly involve working alongside AI-powered systems, robots and automation tools, but humans will still be responsible for diagnosing failures, applying practical knowledge and ensuring work is completed safely.At Ford, the shift is already underway. The automaker employs more than 10,000 skilled-trades workers, representing roughly 20% of its 56,000 UAW-represented workforce. Many of these workers now spend less time maintaining traditional mechanical equipment and more time working with robots, automated production systems and digital manufacturing technologies.Farley said technological advances are making it increasingly difficult to distinguish between engineering roles and skilled trades positions inside modern factories.“The visible line now, it's kind of hard to tell when an engineer or a manufacturing engineer stops, and the skilled trade starts in these newer type operations,” he said.In newer Ford plants, skilled-trades employees may maintain robotic casting systems, troubleshoot battery manufacturing equipment or configure digital production processes. Some tasks, Farley noted, increasingly resemble work performed in semiconductor manufacturing facilities rather than traditional automotive factories.Farley said this shift is already visible on Ford's own factory floors. The company currently employs more than 10,000 skilled-trades workers, representing roughly 20% of its 56,000 UAW workforce. Increasingly, that work is moving beyond traditional maintenance of conveyors and mechanical systems toward repairing robots, handling fiber optic systems, maintaining automated equipment, and operating within increasingly digitized manufacturing environments.He noted that the boundary between skilled trades and engineering has become genuinely blurry inside Ford's newer manufacturing operations, where skilled-trades workers now maintain large robotic casting systems, configure digital manufacturing processes, and troubleshoot equipment used in battery production — work Farley compared more closely to semiconductor fabrication than to a traditional auto plant.Despite the productivity benefits, Farley acknowledged that workers may be sceptical if they believe AI tools are being used for surveillance or could threaten their jobs.Ford already uses AI-powered vision systems to help inspect vehicle components and improve manufacturing quality. However, Farley stressed that companies must ensure workers trust how data generated by those systems is used.“If they don't trust that the data's going to be used the right way, somehow against them or somehow in a not-so-nice way, it's going to be a problem,” he said.Farley framed the current anxiety around AI in manufacturing as a modern version of a much older dynamic: the historical skepticism workers have shown toward time-and-motion studies, an industrial management practice built around timing workers' tasks to identify efficiency improvements. He recalled a personal experience early in his career conducting time-and-motion studies, when a worker several years older than him confronted him during a break after noticing he was being timed, directly accusing him of trying to take his job.Farley said he doesn't see today's AI-driven efficiency tools as fundamentally different from that earlier tension between management's view of a system as an efficiency tool and workers' instinct to see it as surveillance or a threat to their livelihood — suggesting that managing trust, not just deploying the technology itself, will determine how smoothly AI integrates into skilled-trades work going forward.
Article Summary: Ford CEO Jim Farley has made a clear distinction between the types of jobs artificial intelligence is likely to replace and the ones that will remain dependent on human expertise. He argued that skilled trades workers will largely be protected from the first wave of AI disruption. However, he warned that more routine white-collar roles face greater disruption.

Article Title: White House Accord on Super Intelligence that Silicon Valley's top executives hailed as 'historic concord' may have Mark Zuckerberg's 'stamp'
Article Text:
Mark Zuckerberg (Image: ANI)

How Mark Zuckerberg shaped the AI agreement

What the White House AI accord says

Mark Zuckerberg’s changing relationship with Washington

Mark Zuckerberg may be the architect behind a major artificial intelligence (AI) agreement between the White House and some of the biggest companies. According to a Semafor report, the idea for what became US President Donald Trump’s “White House Accord on Super Intelligence” came from a previous conversation between him, Zuckerberg and US House Speaker Mike Johnson at last week’s state dinner. Facebook-parent Meta's chief executive reportedly discussed AI regulation concerns with Johnson before speaking with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang about creating principles technology companies could present to Trump. Zuckerberg then circulated a draft ahead of the recent meeting, which Meta, OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, Google and NVIDIA eventually signed. The White House and participating executives hailed the agreement as a “historic concord” among rival companies, while reports say Zuckerberg played a central role in shaping the pact.The report claims Zuckerberg sat next to Johnson at the state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping. During their conversation, the Meta CEO raised regulatory concerns around AI.He then spoke with Huang about developing common principles that AI companies could agree on before their meeting with Trump. Zuckerberg subsequently circulated a draft of the proposed agreement.Huang also helped gather support for the document among executives attending the White House meeting, including leaders from OpenAI, Anthropic and xAI.Trump eventually released the document as the “White House Accord on Super Intelligence.”Two other sources familiar with the discussions also confirmed Zuckerberg’s central role in shaping the document, Semafor reported. Meta and the White House did not comment on the report.The agreement, signed by Meta, OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, Google and Nvidia, commits the companies to establishing “robust internal controls” and using outside audits to help ensure the safety of frontier AI models.However, the roughly 300-word agreement does not provide extensive details on how those safety controls would work or how companies would be held accountable. It is also not a legally binding regulation.The document does suggest that federal AI regulation could become necessary in the future. Zuckerberg described the agreement as “good steps forward” during the recent meeting“The idea isn’t that this is the only thing that we will ever do. It is that this is a start and an accord that the whole industry could come to,” Zuckerberg told reporters outside the White House Tuesday, appearing alongside Trump, Johnson and others who attended the meeting.The reported role in the agreement comes after a major shift in Zuckerberg’s relationship with Washington. Meta previously faced intense scrutiny from lawmakers over issues including election interference, privacy, content moderation and children’s online safety.Zuckerberg testified before Congress multiple times following the 2016 presidential election. Meta later faced litigation from the federal government and private parties, making the company a major target of scrutiny directed at Big Tech.The relationship with the Trump administration has since changed. Meta suspended Trump from Facebook and Instagram following the January 6 Capitol riot, but the company has subsequently adopted a more cooperative approach toward the administration.The report claimed that Zuckerberg’s involvement in developing the accord shows how his efforts to build closer ties with Trump may have increased his influence over AI policy discussions. It also puts his role alongside Huang and Elon Musk, who have separately developed close relationships with Trump.
Article Summary: Mark Zuckerberg may be the architect behind a major artificial intelligence (AI) agreement between the White House and some of the biggest companies. According to a Semafor report, the idea for what became US President Donald Trump’s “White House Accord on Super Intelligence” came from a previous conversation between him, Zuckerberg and US House Speaker Mike Johnson. Facebook-parent Meta's chief executive reportedly discussed AI regulation concerns with Johnson before speaking with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang about creating principles technology companies could present to Trump. Zuckerberg subsequently circulated a draft of the proposed agreement.

Article Title: Google-parent Alphabet to send in-house AI chips into Orbit on SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket
Article Text:
What is Project Suncatcher , Google’s orbital AI test

Tapping sunlight and satellite swarms

Google-parent company Alphabet is preparing to send its proprietary artificial intelligence (AI) semiconductors into orbit aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket, marking an initial operational step toward evaluating whether supercomputing facilities can operate in space. The uncrewed launch is slated for 11:15 am PT Thursday, October 1 (12:45 am IST, October 2) from California's Vandenberg Air Force Base in Santa Barbara County.The mission, flying under SpaceX’s Transporter-18 rideshare program, carries satellites from Planet Labs, including a solar-powered prototype system fitted with Google’s custom-built Tensor Processing Units (TPUs).The launch represents the inaugural orbital demonstration for Project Suncatcher, an experimental “moonshot” program Alphabet initially introduced in November 2025. Through the initiative, the company wants to assess whether autonomous, solar-powered computing networks can reliably handle heavy machine learning tasks from low Earth orbit.In a statement outlining the launch, Alphabet framed the mission as a pathway to investigate whether orbit can eventually support scalable machine learning infrastructure.The Mountain View tech giant previously evaluated the performance of its TPUs under simulated conditions at a University of California, Davis test facility.However, engineers have yet to measure how the silicon handles the harsher, unfiltered operational environment of space.Orbit offers compelling energy advantages alongside distinct physical challenges. According to the company, satellites traveling in low Earth orbit benefit from near-constant solar exposure, capturing as much as eight times the solar energy available on the Earth's surface.The launch highlights a relationship between Alphabet and SpaceX. While the two technology firms compete aggressively in the AI sector, they maintain tight commercial and investment connections. Alphabet serves as a major stakeholder in SpaceX, which went public in June through a record-breaking initial public offering. Alphabet’s equity in the aerospace firm is valued at more than $82 billion.SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has backed off-planet data hubs as the ultimate solution to land, energy and environmental restrictions on the ground, calling orbital facilities “infinite real estate.” Musk previously claimed that training AI models in space would emerge as the most cost-effective approach within two to three years.Despite the optimism from tech executives, aerospace and computing specialists warn that putting data centers into space remains a highly speculative feat. Key technical and operational bottlenecks include rocket freight capacity which remains tightly constrained and expensive.The second is that electronics in orbit face extreme thermal fluctuations and cosmic radiation, requiring specialised cooling mechanisms and radiation-hardened shielding. Thirdly, growing space junk and orbital clutter present collision hazards for expansive satellite arrays.
Article Summary: Google-parent company Alphabet preparing to send its proprietary artificial intelligence (AI) semiconductors into orbit aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket. The uncrewed launch is slated for 11:15 am PT Thursday, October 1 (12:45 am IST, October 2) from California's Vandenberg Air Force Base in Santa Barbara County.

Article Title: As global race heats up, report claims that China-linked hackers impersonating US government officials
Article Text:
Representative image

Hackers impersonating White House leadership and Anthropic staff

At a time when the tech rivalry between Washington and Beijing is intensifying, suspected Chinese state-aligned cyber operatives have reportedly launched a targeted social-engineering campaign, posing as former US government officials and leading private-sector researchers to steal sensitive insights on American artificial intelligence (AI) policy. According to findings published on Thursday (October 1) by Silicon Valley cybersecurity company Proofpoint, the espionage operation specifically targeted prominent US specialists focused on military applications of AI and semiconductor export controls.The targets included analysts, legal counsel, and academic scholars across American universities, national security think tanks, and law firms, the findings claim (via CNN). Gaining access to the personal accounts and correspondence of these experts may hand Beijing an inside look at how American institutions are debating national security guardrails, trade curbs and regulatory frameworks around cutting-edge machine learning.While Proofpoint confirmed it found no clear traces of compromised corporate systems, researchers cautioned that they may have uncovered only a slice of the intrusion attempts.“We are confident that [the hacking group] is a Chinese government-aligned threat actor based on targeting consistently in line with Chinese government interests, observed infrastructure and technical artifacts, and corroboration from industry partners,” Proofpoint staff researcher Mark Kelly told CNN.The cyber operators deployed targeted deception campaigns across two distinct windows in February and July, adopting the identities of prominent figures in the artificial intelligence sector. They posed as a former White House tech advisor, fabricating communications purporting to come from Lynne Parker, who previously served as a senior White House technology policy director under both Donald Trump and Joe Biden.These cybercriminals reportedly also impersonated a senior team member at AI startup Anthropic, which had recently sparred with the White House over deployment guardrails. On February 26, the attackers sent an email titled “Request for Feedback on Military Integration of Claude” to an AI analyst at a US think tank, attempting to harvest login credentials.Parker, now associate vice chancellor emerita at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, said colleagues alerted her after receiving suspicious emails bearing her identity:“My first concern was for the colleagues who might receive the impersonated email. I wanted to warn them but realized that’s very difficult to do when I don’t know who is being targeted. On a personal level, I felt sadness that relationships I’ve built over my career were being exploited by bad actors to deceive others,” Parker told CNN.She stressed that defensive measures must protect the individuals shaping the country’s regulatory and strategic frameworks.
Article Summary: Chinese state-aligned cyber operatives reportedly launched a targeted social- engineering campaign. They posed as former US government officials and leading private-sector researchers to steal sensitive insights on American artificial intelligence (AI) policy. Gaining access to the personal accounts and correspondence of these experts may hand Beijing an inside look at how American institutions are debating national security guardrails, trade curbs and regulatory frameworks.

Article Title: Apple Pay’s India challenge: Finding room in a UPI-first market
Article Text:
Apple Pay

The opportunity is in cards, not QR codes

Scale will depend on what comes next

Apple Pay has finally come to India, more than a decade after its global debut. But it is arriving in a payments market vastly different from the one in which Apple originally built the service.India does not need convincing about paying with a phone. From a roadside tea stall to a supermarket checkout, QR codes and UPI have already made the smartphone a wallet. UPI accounts for the overwhelming majority of digital-payment transactions in the country. Apple’s challenge, therefore, is not to introduce mobile payments to India. It is to convince a section of Indians that there is a better way to use their cards. That explains the deliberately narrow start.Apple Pay has launched initially with Axis Bank-issued Visa and Mastercard credit cards, allowing customers to add eligible cards to Apple Wallet and tap an iPhone or Apple Watch at a compatible NFC terminal, or use Apple Pay during checkout in supported apps and websites. Other banks are expected to be added as partnerships and technical integrations fall into place.The starting pool is small compared with UPI. But that may not be the right comparison.Apple Pay does not need to replace the QR code at the neighbourhood store to establish a meaningful business in India. Credit-card usage has been rising alongside UPI. India had more than 124 million credit cards outstanding in August, with monthly spending of about Rs 2 lakh crore. Axis Bank alone had over 16 million cards, making it one of the country’s largest issuers.That market also overlaps neatly with Apple’s customer base. iPhones remain concentrated towards the premium end of India’s smartphone market, where users are more likely to own credit cards, transact at organised retail, travel frequently and shop online.For these users, Apple Pay is less another payments app and more a way of removing friction from an existing behaviour. A physical card no longer needs to come out of the wallet. In an app or on a website, users do not have to repeatedly enter card details. At a shop, payment can be authenticated on the device using Face ID, Touch ID or the passcode before tapping at an NFC-enabled terminal.The timing also matters. Apple is entering India after contactless card infrastructure has become far more widespread and consumers have grown accustomed to using their phones for everyday payments. That gives Apple Pay a more receptive market than it would have found a few years ago — even if the behaviour it is trying to tap remains very different from the QR-led payments habit built by UPI.Apple is initially taking Apple Pay to thousands of merchants across categories including food and beverage, travel, fashion and lifestyle. The merchant network includes Tata and Reliance brands, Chaayos, Interflora, Le15, Comet, House of Masaba and Apple Stores.On the digital-commerce side, Apple Pay will be available on apps including Blinkit, Ixigo, MakeMyTrip, Zepto and Zomato. In other words, Apple is starting where its users are most likely to encounter the service rather than trying immediately to replicate UPI’s extraordinary ubiquity. The bigger question is how quickly that circle expands.For now, an iPhone user who does not have an eligible Axis Bank card cannot use Apple Pay. RuPay is not supported at launch either. By comparison, UPI lets consumers link accounts across a wide set of banks and use essentially the same payment method across millions of merchants.Apple therefore faces a classic network problem: The service becomes more useful with every additional bank, card network and merchant that joins it. The company is looking to add more issuing banks over time, depending on their technical readiness and card portfolios. That expansion will matter more than the headline launch itself. If Apple Pay remains confined to a relatively narrow set of cards, it risks becoming a useful but niche feature. If major banks come on board quickly, the addressable base expands sharply.There is another important distinction. Apple Pay and UPI solve somewhat different problems. UPI turned bank accounts into an extraordinarily low-friction payment instrument and built acceptance without requiring merchants to install card terminals. Apple Pay, at least in its current Indian form, sits on top of the existing card ecosystem. It makes that ecosystem easier to use rather than bypassing it. That could leave room for both.A consumer may continue scanning a QR code for a small everyday purchase, use Apple Pay with a rewards credit card at a restaurant and choose Apple Pay during an online purchase where otherwise card details and authentication would have added extra steps.That is also why Apple Pay’s India opportunity may be strongest in categories where cards already have a meaningful role — organised retail, travel, food delivery, fashion, hotels and higher-value purchases — rather than in the small-ticket transactions where UPI has become almost instinctive.For Apple, that may be enough. Apple Pay does not have to become India’s biggest payment system to deepen the role of the iPhone and Apple Watch in a user’s daily life. It strengthens the broader Apple ecosystem by making another routine activity happen inside its devices and Wallet.The eventual test, then, is unlikely to be whether Apple Pay can beat UPI. It is whether Apple can make using a credit card through an iPhone or Apple Watch feel easier than pulling the card out itself. India has already embraced paying by phone. Apple’s job now is to persuade its users that, sometimes, tapping can be easier than scanning.
Article Summary: India does not need convincing about paying with a phone. Apple’s challenge is not to introduce mobile payments to India. It is to convince a section of Indians that there is a better way to use their cards. Apple is entering India after contactless card infrastructure has become far more widespread.

Apple's next big launch is not an iPhone. The company is set to enter the smart home category on October 13 with its first-ever smart display, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman. The device, code-named J490 inside Apple and widely referred to as the "HomePad," will arrive alongside a refreshed HomePod mini and a new Apple TV 4K.All three products are built to showcase Siri AI, the overhauled assistant Apple released with iOS 27 last month. The hub is Apple's most direct answer yet to Amazon's Echo Show and Google's Nest Hub, and one of the first big launches under John Ternus , who took over as CEO in September.It is still unclear whether October 13 is an announcement or a sales date. Apple Stores have reportedly received boxes marked "Do Not Open Until October 8," pointing to new in-store displays. Apple has not commented, and pricing, including for India, is yet to surface.The countertop model has a roughly 6-inch square screen with rounded corners and quarter-inch black bezels, much like older iPads. It is about as thick as an iPhone and is held up by a polished metal arm on a round aluminium base lined with rings of speaker holes.The look recalls the 2002 iMac G4, and the screen tilts forward and backward by hand.There is no battery, so it stays plugged in over USB-C, and there are no volume or power buttons. A single front-facing camera handles FaceTime calls and recognition. It comes in Apple's standard grey aluminium finish with a rubberised bottom to keep it steady on a table.A wall-mounted version swaps the round base for a thin square one that sits flat below the screen and houses the speakers and microphones. Apple is also developing a larger model with the display on a robotic arm.Personalisation is the big draw. Using its camera and microphones, the hub identifies who is standing in front of it or speaking, then pulls up that person's messages, calendar, notes and preferred widgets. When someone else walks up, the screen switches over, and a visitor mode hides personal data from guests.Bloomberg says the face recognition is less secure than Face ID, so users can require confirmation on their iPhone before sensitive information appears.Apple expects households to buy more than one. The hubs can control lights and thermostats, work as intercoms between rooms, play music and podcasts, and cycle through iCloud photos. Employees are already testing them widely at home.The hub runs a new operating system built around Siri AI. It mixes iPad-style two-panel apps such as Messages with Apple Watch-like icon grids, plus clock and photo faces similar to the upgraded StandBy mode on the iPhone Duo. Calendar, Photos, FaceTime, Notes, Reminders, Music and Podcasts are among the built-in apps, and users can rearrange apps and widgets with a long press.Apple had planned a home display as early as 2024 but held it back until Siri could carry the product. Users will be able to ask it to find a song someone shared weeks ago, pull up a specific photo, or complete tasks inside Notes and Calendar.The HomePod mini gets its first hardware update since its 2020 debut. The design stays, but a faster processor lets it run Apple's newer AI models, and green and pink join the colour options.The Apple TV 4K, last refreshed in 2022, follows the same playbook with an unchanged exterior and a quicker chip. Leaked data also points to Apple's N1 wireless chip with Wi-Fi 7 support and a revised Siri Remote.At his first keynote as CEO last month, Ternus pitched the iPhone as the ideal AI device. The home hub carries that pitch to the kitchen counter and the living-room wall, a space Amazon and Google have had largely to themselves for nearly a decade.
Article Summary: Apple set to enter smart home category on October 13 with its first-ever smart display. The device, code-named J490 inside Apple and widely referred to as the "HomePad," will arrive alongside a refreshed HomePod mini and a new Apple TV 4K. All three products are built to showcase Siri AI, the overhauled assistant Apple released with iOS 27 last month.

Article Title: Google DeepMind watermarks AI-generated protein as company chief AI scientist Demis Hassabis flags Biosecurity as urgent AI-era challenge
Article Text:
‘An urgent challenge for the AI era’

How SynthID Bio operates

In what can be called a major breakthrough for synthetic biology and AI-powered biosecurity, Google DeepMind, Google’s AI lab, has developed a new method to watermark AI-designed proteins, establishing a permanent proof of origin directly inside biological code. Published in the journal Nature, the proof-of-concept technology, which is named SynthID Bio, solves a long-standing technical challenge: embedding an non-noticeable, verifiable digital identifier into biological sequences and predicted molecular structures without degrading their physical real-world utility in laboratory tests.The rollout comes amid rapid advancements in biological machine learning, where systems like AlphaFold 3, AlphaProteo and ProteinMPNN allow scientists to predict complex folding patterns and engineer functional binders. Yet these generative capabilities have heightened global biosecurity risks. Unfamiliar, machine-generated sequences can slip past conventional gene-synthesis filters, while unverified synthetic structural data risks contaminating open-access scientific repositories.Google DeepMind Chief AI Scientist Demis Hassabis emphasised that guarding against biological misuse must be treated as a frontline safety priority for frontier AI:“Biosecurity is one of the most urgent challenges for the AI era. Bringing SynthID to biology so AI-generated proteins can be watermarked is a critical step - and we’re open sourcing SynthID Bio tools so the research community can build on this work. Published in @Nature today, congrats to the team!”Pushmeet Kohli, Vice President of Science at Google DeepMind and Chief Scientist at Google Cloud, celebrated the practical synthesis of these molecules:“Very happy to announce that our team at Google DeepMind has pushed the boundaries of generative biology, achieving the successful synthesis of AI-designed proteins that are both functional and watermarked.This proof-of-concept watermarking of the building blocks of life is enabled by SynthID Bio, our new protein watermarking method. It is designed to safeguard the new era of AI-powered generative biology and strengthen global biosecurity. ”SynthID Bio functions as a modular toolkit tailored across two primary dimensions of structural biology:SynthIDBio-sequence that subtly steers the selection of amino acid building blocks during sequence generation. In laboratory validation, watermarked protein binders engineered via AlphaProteo and a customized version of ProteinMPNN exhibited binding affinities on par with unmarked variants, while maintaining near-perfect watermark identification rates.SynthIDBio-structure relies on a fine-tuned iteration of AlphaFold 3 to insert an imperceptible mathematical watermark across atomic coordinate arrays, leaving a dependable detection signal without warping the molecular conformation.The signature persists beyond the digital blueprint: it remains fully detectable on the physical, synthesized protein itself after wet-lab manufacturing.
Article Summary: Google DeepMind has developed a new method to watermark AI-designed proteins, establishing a permanent proof of origin directly inside biological code. The technology, named SynthID Bio, solves a long-standing technical challenge: embedding an non-noticeable, verifiable digital identifier into biological sequences.

Article Title: Microsoft co-founder Paul Allen backed a $5 million medical evacuation project after Ebola; in 2020, its technology helped bring 14 Americans with coronavirus home from a cruise ship in Japan
Article Text:
From Ebola to coronavirus

How the system works

Legacy Beyond Technology

A medical evacuation technology backed by late Microsoft co-founder Paul Allen after the 2014 Ebola outbreak went on to play a crucial role during the early days of the Covid-19 pandemic, helping safely transport infected Americans from a quarantined cruise ship in Japan. Following the Ebola crisis in West Africa, Allen provided $5 million in funding to support the development of advanced biocontainment capabilities that could safely move patients infected with highly contagious diseases. The project led to the creation of specialised isolation systems designed to protect both patients and medical personnel during transport.The technology called Containerized Biocontainment System (CBCS) was developed by Kansas City-based biocontainment and global health engineering firm MRIGlobal with the help of a public-private partnership with the US Department of State and the Paul G. Allen Foundation, created in direct response to the 2014 West African Ebola outbreak. At that time the world was witnessing a pressing need for a way to safely transport the infected patients over long distances without risking the lives of the flight crew, medical staff or the general public.After many years that same system was being used at the centre of the first major medical evacuations of the COVID-19 pandemic.On February 17, 2020, around 14 US citizens who tested positive for Coronavirus were evacuated from the Diamond Princess cruise ship, which had been under quarantine off Japan's coast for more than 10 days. Instead of remaining stranded from home, the patients were transported in specialised containment units on a chartered evacuation aircraft, which isolated them using standard biosafety protocols en route to coronavirus treatment centers in the US.MRIGlobal engineered the CBCS as a reusable, flight-ready biocontainment and medical treatment unit designed to roll on and off government or civilian cargo aircraft. The units are built to containerize highly contagious pathogens, are described as extremely durable, and are specifically designed to allow the safe transport of critically ill patients while maintaining both biocontainment integrity and safe flight conditions. Dean Gray, director at MRIGlobal, said the organization was proud to play a role in helping safely evacuate people out of harm's way to locations where they could receive appropriate medical care. He added that there's nothing quite like the CBCS for flyable medical transport, noting that it was developed specifically to respond to critical global health emergencies like the coronavirus outbreak, with the ultimate goal of saving lives.As of the February 2020 evacuation, MRIGlobal had designed and delivered four CBCS units, all in active use by the US government. The system's significance was recognized well before the pandemic, too — it received an R&D 100 Award for Innovation from R&D Magazine in 2016, an honor given annually to 100 of the most technologically significant innovations introduced to the marketplace that year.While Allen is best known for co-founding Microsoft alongside Bill Gates, his contributions extended into scientific research, public health and disaster response. The successful deployment of the biocontainment transport system during the Covid-19 pandemic demonstrated how investments made years earlier in response to Ebola helped address an entirely different global health emergency.
Article Summary: The Containerized Biocontainment System (CBCS) was developed in response to the 2014 West African Ebola outbreak. Allen provided $5 million in funding to support the development of advanced biocont containment capabilities that could safely move patients infected with highly contagious diseases. After many years that same system was being used at the centre of the first major medical evacuations of the COVID-19 pandemic.

Article Title: Jensen Huang 'confronts' Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on his AI statements that have made Nvidia CEO very upset
Article Text:
Jensen Huang 'confronts' Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on his AI statements that have made Nvidia CEO very upset

Why Jensen Huang questioned Dario Amodei

Tech CEOs agree to safety principles

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and other technology executives privately questioned Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei over his public warnings about the risks of artificial intelligence. According to a Wall Street Journal (WDJ) report, the discussion took place on September 29 after nearly two dozen CEOs met Trump for lunch and agreed to a set of voluntary principles for safer AI development. During the luncheon, tech executives including Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang reportedly asked Dario Amodei why he was being so extreme in public about AI capabilities and the risks they could create. Amodei defended his position, saying it was important to be honest with the public and not play down the risks.Jensen Huang has pushed back against AI warnings saying: “Don’t think for a second just because you’re an alarmist that you’re doing a social good. It is not true. I think that we ought to just all be wiser, more mature, be evidence based, be scientific”.The private discussion highlights a growing difference among major AI companies over how quickly the technology should develop and how much attention should be given to its risks.Dario Amodei has repeatedly warned about the possible dangers of advanced AI, including cyberattacks and large-scale job losses.He has also criticised the White House and some technology companies for playing down those risks.At Tuesday's meeting, Amodei told other executives that the public should be given an accurate picture of what AI models can do and the risks they pose, according to people familiar with the discussion cited by the WSJ.Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson brought the AI executives together as pressure grows over the safety of increasingly capable AI systems. The companies agreed to work with independent auditors and establish stronger internal controls to check whether their AI systems operate as intended. They also agreed to work to prevent AI tools from hacking or accessing technical systems in unintended ways.The agreement came after reports of AI agents behaving unexpectedly and accessing other systems, adding to calls for stronger safety testing. Mark Zuckerberg also pushed back against Dario’s AI warningsMeta CEO Mark Zuckerberg also responded to Amodei's concerns during the lunch, according to the WSJ. Mark Zuckerberg reportedly argued that the best way to address the concerns was for the industry to follow through on the safety principles being developed.
Article Summary: Jensen Huang 'confronted' Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei over his public warnings about the risks of artificial intelligence. The discussion took place after nearly two dozen CEOs met Trump for lunch and agreed to a set of voluntary principles for safer AI development.
